name: sqlite_query
description: Run a read-only SQL query over a SQLite database file through Python's sqlite3 module and an authorizer that allows reading only (no write, ATTACH, extension or setting pragma), and return typed rows: an inline page (limit, and a byte ceiling) and, when the result is more, the whole of it as JSON Lines in rows_file. NULL is null, a BLOB is {blob_b64, length, sha256}, text that is not UTF-8 keeps its bytes. The database is opened immutable: a -wal or -shm beside it is inventoried (size, sha256, WAL frames) but NOT applied, so a row committed only in the WAL is missing from the result, which snapshot_status says; a hot rollback journal is said too. To read the state with the WAL applied, run sqlite_snapshot (it copies the set with hashes and has SQLite apply the WAL in the copy) and give its directory or its `database` as db_path: the answer then carries `snapshot` (what it holds, and whether the file queried still matches the receipt's sha256) and snapshot_status says which state the rows are; apply_wal is not a parameter here and asking for it is an error that names sqlite_snapshot. Several statements run one by one. A file that is not SQLite is reported with its first bytes (not in write_values mode) and entropy: high entropy is not identified, and encryption is one explanation among others. It does not recover deleted records or read unallocated pages. VALUES TO A FILE: with write_values true (only in a job run with secret_output true; refused outside one before anything is opened) the tool takes table, and optionally columns, rowid_from and rowid_to, instead of sql, and writes the values of that one table to a 0600 file under $OUT (sqlite-query-values.jsonl, created exclusively and never followed through a link once the table is found and before its first row: a wrong name leaves nothing, a second export in the same job is refused as JSON; its last line is an end line, so a file cut short is recognisable) and puts none of them in the answer: the answer carries each cell's locator, type and length, per-column counts, the first rows, and locators_file with every row (bounded at 2 GiB, said). There is no sql in this mode on purpose: a WHERE, LIKE or JOIN over a column whose values are withheld would confirm a guess one call at a time, so the mode exports whole rows, reads them from the table itself and never through an index, and takes no filter. What locates a row (table_kind): on an ordinary rowid table the rowid, which is no column's value (SQLite assigns it unless the application set it), in rowid order, and rowid_from/rowid_to select by it; on a table whose one primary key column is declared INTEGER the rowid IS that column's value, so it is never printed, a rowid range is refused (rowid_is_a_value) and rows are located by their position n, which ranks the key's values; on a WITHOUT ROWID table n follows the primary key's order and so ranks its values too; a virtual table is located by n (fts5 may be the named state virtual_table_unsupported on some SQLite builds). A number's length is the characters of its decimal form (its order of magnitude). sqlite's own error message is never printed (a generated column's error can quote a value): the answer gives the class and the row, the values file the message; a cell over the 64 MiB length limit (value_too_large) or one sqlite cannot compute (unreadable) is listed and the export goes on; a write that fails (a full disk) is said as JSON (values_file_error, complete false, exit 0) and the partial file is kept without its end line. No hash or fragment of a value is printed, and a printed file, table or column name shaped like a token is withheld. Only tables are read (not views). earlier_answers says how many other files answer the same question (a different answer is kept as name.2.jsonl, never over the first).

db_path.description: Path to the SQLite database file (the main file; a -wal beside it is reported, not applied), or the directory of a sqlite_snapshot, or the database inside one (its WAL is then applied in that copy).

sql.description: One or more SQL statements: SELECT, WITH, VALUES, EXPLAIN, or a PRAGMA that only reports. Required unless write_values is true, where it is refused.

csv.description: Render stdout, the text of the inline page, as CSV with a header (default: the shell's |-separated list without one).

limit.description: Rows in the inline page (default 100, at most 10000); the whole result is in rows_file when it is more. With write_values the page holds locators, and locators_file has every row.

max_seconds.description: Stop the query after this long (default 25, at most 110); the rows before it are kept and the result says it stopped.

readonly.description: Accepted only as true: this tool never opens a database for writing.

write_values.description: Write the values of one table to a 0600 file under $OUT instead of returning them (a job run with secret_output true; refused outside a job). Takes table, not sql. The answer carries locators, types, lengths and counts, never a value.

table.description: With write_values: the table whose cells go to the values file (a table, not a view).

columns.description: With write_values: the columns to export (default: every column of the table).

rowid_from.description: With write_values, on an ordinary rowid table (table_kind rowid): the first rowid to export (inclusive). The rowid there is no column's value; on a table whose rowid is a column's value (INTEGER PRIMARY KEY), a WITHOUT ROWID or a virtual table a range is refused.

rowid_to.description: With write_values, on an ordinary rowid table: the last rowid to export (inclusive).
